## What is the problem this feature will solve?

Node.js currently starts with no visual acknowledgement when invoked without a script. Developers who use Node.js interactively or in terminal demos have no built-in, opt-in way to display the runtime version and a compact Node.js identity banner.

## What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add an opt-in CLI flag, such as `node --splash`, that writes a compact ANSI splash banner to stdout before entering the REPL. The banner would include a Node.js wordmark, `process.version`, and a short tagline. It should only emit color when the output is a TTY and color is enabled, honor existing color controls such as `NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR`, avoid output when Node.js executes a script or receives piped input, and add no startup overhead unless explicitly requested.

## What alternatives have you considered?

A userland script can print a banner (for example, `node ~/splash.js`), but it requires a separate command and cannot integrate with Node.js CLI color, TTY, and REPL behavior. Shell aliases and third-party REPL wrappers have the same limitation. Keeping the behavior behind an explicit flag avoids changing established CLI output.
issues.title: feat: add an optional Node.js CLI splash banner

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Almost all operating systems enable Address Space Layout Randomisation (ASLR) to help prevent memory-related vulnerabilities from reaching a state where Remote Code Execution (RCE) is possible.

To take full advantage of this protection, an executable must be compiled as a Position Independent Executable (PIE).

The current state of PIE in Node.js is as follows:

- ✅ macOS - PIE since 2020 via https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/35704

- ⏳ Windows - PIE via `/DYNAMICBASE` being proposed at https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/64212

- ✅ Linux using musl libc - PIE is compiler default for all executables
  
- ✅ Linux using glibc where `node` binary is compiled and provided by OS package manager - PIE is default for almost all OS-level package repositories

- ❌ Linux using glibc where `node` binary is provided by Node.js - Not PIE


### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

A [previous discussion from May 2020](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/33425) rejected use of PIE on Linux due to a expected performance penalty of 5-10% and, at that point in time, little evidence of RCE within the Node.js ecosystem.

Given many organisations already quite happily use Node.js with PIE/ASLR, be that on macOS, via Alpine Linux based containers or OS-provided packages, is it time to revisit this discussion for those left behind?

The performance impact of PIE is negligible on 64-bit ARM CPUs, which have seen increasing adoption since 2020 e.g. AWS Graviton.

Do the security benefits of PIE now outweigh the performance cost for those still running glibc-based Linux on x64 architecture CPUs?

By way of a recent example, had this change already been in place then it's likely [CVE-2026-111497](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35) would have been rated "High" rather than "Critical" severity.


### What alternatives have you considered?

If there's still a desire to provide official binaries for a subset of platforms without PIE then perhaps offering a security-hardened alternative with PIE might help raise awareness.
issues.title: Proposal: build official Node.js binaries for glibc-based Linux using PIE, enables ASLR, helps prevent RCE

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

An application that reads a YAML config file needs a third-party parser. Should Node provide one directly? If so, should it live in its own module?

YAML also came up in #53787, the discussion about Node's own configuration file. 

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

#67157 proposes one function behind `--experimental-yaml`:

```js
import { parse } from 'node:yaml';

parse('port: 8080'); // { port: 8080 }
```

Whether the parser is written in JS, vendored from `yaml` or `js-yaml`, or built in C++ or wasm is discussed in the PR, with measurements; the API is the same in every case. This issue is about the API.

- `parse(input[, options])` accepts a string or UTF-8 bytes in an `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer`, typed array or `DataView`.
- One document returns its value, multiple documents return an array, and an empty stream returns `null`.
- Invalid YAML throws a `SyntaxError` with code `ERR_INVALID_YAML` and a line and column. With `throwIfInvalid: false`, it returns `undefined` instead.
- The parser uses the YAML 1.2 core schema: `yes` and `no` are strings, and `0777` is decimal. It doesn't convert timestamps to dates, expand merge keys or decode `!!binary`.
- Mappings become plain objects. Even `__proto__` is an own property. Duplicate keys are errors. Aliases to a collection refer to the same object, so the result can contain cycles.

Possible follow-ups:

- `stringify(value[, replacer[, space]])`, with arguments like `JSON.stringify()`.
- A `version` option. Should we reserve it now with `'1.2'` as the only supported value, or wait until there's a second version to choose from?
- A `reviver` option to transform parsed values. We'd need to define how it visits shared references and cycles.
- A file or stream API that can parse large inputs without keeping the whole source in memory.

I'd favor `node:yaml` if we expect to offer both parsing and stringifying. It keeps those operations together. One concern raised in review is whether that sets a precedent for a module per format. I'd judge TOML, XML and other formats on their own use cases.


### What alternatives have you considered?

1. Add `util.parseYAML()` alongside `util.parseEnv()`. This seems like a good fit if parsing is all we want.
2. Use a shared module such as `node:serdes`, with `serdes.yaml.parse()`. Other formats could use it later, but we'd be designing the shared API with only one format in mind.
3. Keep YAML internal if Node adopts it for a feature such as config files or `import config from './config.yaml' with { type: 'yaml' }`. Applications would still choose their own parser.
4. Leave YAML to packages such as `yaml` and `js-yaml`. Users can already choose between them, and core wouldn't take on another parser to maintain.
issues.title: Proposal: built-in YAML support, public API and placement

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Hey 👋

Currently, the only way to tell whether a prepared `Statement` returns rows is `statement.columns().length > 0`, which is great when you also need the column metadata, except when all you need is a yes/no. `columns()` builds a metadata object per column, so it gets slower the wider the result set is.

Query builders and ORMs need this answer on every execution, to pick `all()` vs `run()`. Kysely does it for raw SQL, where `insert ... returning` and friends can't be classified from the query alone (https://github.com/kysely-org/kysely/issues/1292). Knex, TypeORM and Prisma 7 do it for every query:

https://github.com/knex/knex/blob/e25d54bcb707714a17f5a5744eba5c4246bb4d1d/lib/dialects/better-sqlite3/index.js#L51
https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/blob/5a572a40bae2f85a1d5f7b87a0aa88bbbaec5ab3/packages/typeorm/src/driver/better-sqlite3/BetterSqlite3QueryRunner.ts#L122
https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/0b596ffecfcc55e37d6a7095c03193e2d28b8090/packages/adapter-better-sqlite3/src/better-sqlite3.ts#L110

These integrations were written against `better-sqlite3`, which exposes it as a `reader` boolean, computed once at prepare time from `sqlite3_column_count`:

https://github.com/WiseLibs/better-sqlite3/blob/dbc2ea1165fef1f599b9be12faea33fa5e9d7ffb/src/objects/statement.cpp#L142-L155

On `node:sqlite`, they're left with paying for `columns()` or guessing. Prisma 8 calls `columns()` on every write, and MikroORM 7 fakes `reader` with regexes over the SQL text:

https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/557c0d4c1b1061b8fff954dc96598ff4db95d262/packages/3-targets/sqlite/3-driver/src/sqlite-driver.ts#L85
https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/blob/14737a2349c834dbb39e1dc82bd5adf32fb2531c/packages/sql/src/dialects/sqlite/NodeSqliteDialect.ts#L31

`node:sqlite` already calls `sqlite3_column_count` internally, but only exposes it through `columns()`:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/18b32a3b1552e199a01f1a8d9fd64aa756d3b75b/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4397

`columns().length > 0` on v26.13.0 (darwin-arm64):

```text
insert (0 cols)    20 ns/op
select 1 col      315 ns/op
select 8 cols   2,202 ns/op
select 32 cols  8,653 ns/op
```

For comparison, `prepare()` of the 8 column select is ~5,200 ns/op, and `better-sqlite3`'s `stmt.reader` is ~8 ns/op.

```js
import { Database } from 'node:sqlite'

const db = new Database(':memory:')
db.exec('create table t (id integer primary key, name text, a, b, c, d, e, f)')

const N = 1_000_000
const bench = (label, fn) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 1e5; i++) fn()
  const start = process.hrtime.bigint()
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) fn()
  console.log(label, (Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / N).toFixed(1), 'ns/op')
}

for (const [label, sql] of [
  ['insert (0 cols)', 'insert into t (name) values (?)'],
  ['select 1 col', 'select id from t'],
  ['select 8 cols', 'select * from t'],
  ['select 32 cols', 'select *, *, *, * from t'],
]) {
  const stmt = db.prepare(sql)
  bench(label, () => stmt.columns().length > 0)
}
```

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

A side-effect-free `reader` getter on `Statement`, next to `sourceSQL` and `expandedSQL`, with the same semantics as `better-sqlite3` (`true` when the statement returns data):

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/18b32a3b1552e199a01f1a8d9fd64aa756d3b75b/src/node_sqlite.cc#L4945-L4952

`columns()` itself was added to mirror `better-sqlite3` (#57490). This is purely additive, like `stat()` and `resetStats()` (#64541), and removes one of the differences that keep `better-sqlite3`-based integrations from accepting a `node:sqlite` `Database` as is.

### What alternatives have you considered?

A `columnCount` getter that returns `sqlite3_column_count` as is. It's more general, and `reader` would just be `columnCount > 0`, but integrations written against `better-sqlite3` would have to special-case it.

`sqlite3_stmt_readonly` is not a substitute, `insert ... returning` is not read-only but does return rows.

Classifying the SQL text or the query builder's AST in userland works for builder queries, but not for raw SQL, which is why MikroORM's regexes above can misclassify statements.
issues.title: sqlite: add `reader` to `Statement`, aligned with `better-sqlite3`

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Hey 👋

Currently, `node:sqlite` is close to being a drop-in replacement for `better-sqlite3` in query builders, ORMs and drivers, which is great, except parameters are bound differently. Integrations written against `better-sqlite3` pass parameters as an array, e.g. Kysely, Knex and Prisma 7:

https://github.com/kysely-org/kysely/blob/67263069a242600e914e8a9e03b118e8cbf4267c/src/dialect/sqlite/sqlite-driver.ts#L117
https://github.com/knex/knex/blob/e25d54bcb707714a17f5a5744eba5c4246bb4d1d/lib/dialects/better-sqlite3/index.js#L52
https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/0b596ffecfcc55e37d6a7095c03193e2d28b8090/packages/adapter-better-sqlite3/src/better-sqlite3.ts#L90

`node:sqlite` treats an array as a named parameters object, with keys `'0'`, `'1'`, etc., so none of them can accept a `node:sqlite` `Database` without changes, and wrappers have to adapt every call, e.g. MikroORM 7:

https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/blob/14737a2349c834dbb39e1dc82bd5adf32fb2531c/packages/sql/src/dialects/sqlite/NodeSqliteDialect.ts#L32-L33

`better-sqlite3` flattens arrays into anonymous parameters, in any position, and accepts a single named parameters object in any position:

https://github.com/WiseLibs/better-sqlite3/blob/dbc2ea1165fef1f599b9be12faea33fa5e9d7ffb/src/util/binder.cpp#L165-L186

`node:sqlite` only treats the first argument as a potential named parameters object:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/18b32a3b1552e199a01f1a8d9fd64aa756d3b75b/src/node_sqlite.cc#L3859-L3860

```js
import { Database } from 'node:sqlite'

const db = new Database(':memory:')

db.prepare('select ? as a, ? as b').all([1, 2])
// Error: Unknown named parameter '0'

db.prepare('select ? as a, ? as b, ? as c').all(1, [2, 3])
// Error: Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 2.

db.prepare('select :x as x, ? as a').all(2, { x: 1 })
// Error: Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 3.

const stmt = db.prepare('select ? as a, ? as b')
stmt.setAllowUnknownNamedParameters(true)
stmt.all([1, 2])
// [ { a: null, b: null } ] 😬
```

| | `better-sqlite3` | `node:sqlite` |
|---|---|---|
| `all(1, 2)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `all([1, 2])` | ✅ | ❌ `Unknown named parameter '0'` |
| `all([1, 2], 3)` | ✅ | ❌ `Unknown named parameter '0'` |
| `all(1, [2, 3])` | ✅ | ❌ `Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 2.` |
| `all([1], [2, 3])` | ✅ | ❌ `Unknown named parameter '0'` |
| `all({ x: 1 }, 2)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `all(2, { x: 1 })` | ✅ | ❌ `Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 3.` |
| `all([2, 3], { x: 1 })` | ✅ | ❌ `Unknown named parameter '0'` |
| `all({ x: 1 }, [2, 3])` | ✅ | ❌ `Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 2.` |

This was raised from a different angle (stack size) in #57932, which was closed as stale.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

`all()`, `get()`, `iterate()` and `run()` should bind parameters the same way `better-sqlite3` does: arrays are flattened into anonymous parameters, in any position, and a single plain object, in any position, is named parameters.

Every call shape this changes currently throws, or silently binds `NULL` with `setAllowUnknownNamedParameters(true)`, so no working code relies on the current behavior.

Together with #67352 (`reader`), this lets Kysely's `better-sqlite3` dialect run on a `node:sqlite` `Database` as is: migrations, `insert ... returning`, raw queries, streaming, transactions and introspection all pass with just those two differences shimmed.

### What alternatives have you considered?

Only accepting an array as the first argument. It covers the most common call shape, but integrations that use the other shapes would still need changes.

Spreading in userland, `statement.all(...parameters)`. It works up to SQLite's default limit of 32766 parameters, but it's exactly the downstream change we want to avoid: every `better-sqlite3`-based integration has to special-case `node:sqlite`, and switching their call sites to spread breaks wrappers that implement the array signature.
issues.title: sqlite: bind parameters the same way `better-sqlite3` does.

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Node.js doesn't support a user-configured fallback directory when trying to resolve imports. It only resolves those imports against a `node_modules` directory in the same (or ancestor) directory as the importing file. This current architecture falls short for standalone scripts, which don't have a `node_modules` directory around.

This artificial limitation hinders Node.js's ability to fulfill its goal to "[Run JavaScript Everywhere](https://github.com/nodejs#:~:text=Run%20JavaScript%20Everywhere)".

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Fall back to a user-configured directory when normal resolution fails

### What alternatives have you considered?

- Hardcoding absolute paths using the `file://` protocol
    - fragile
    - not portable
- A symlinked `node_modules` in the importing file's directory
    - overridden once `npm install` is executed
- A symlinked `node_modules` in a shared ancestor directory
    - must be located at the filesystem root to cover every location
- A register hook that retries from a specified directory after an `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`/`MODULE_NOT_FOUND` error
    - must be included in every importing file
    - doesn't work with static imports
    - isn't compatible with tooling (e.g., IDEs don't run it, so they treat the imported modules like unresolved ones)
issues.title: Fall back to a user-configured directory when resolving imports

issues.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/66484 added mkstemp and mkstempSync, which return an object with `path` and `handle` methods. These require manual cleanup:

> The file is not removed automatically. It is the caller's responsibility to close the {FileHandle} and to remove the file when it is no longer needed.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

That object should have a Symbol.dispose method which removes the file when invoked.

As the PR says:

> a disposable variant in the style of fs.mkdtempDisposableSync(). I would leave it for a follow-up, to keep this PR to the plain API.

But mkdtempDisposableSync needed to be a separate API, because it `mkdtempDisposable` returns a bare string. Here it's returning an object and so could be disposable directly, no need for a new API.

### What alternatives have you considered?

_No response_
issues.title: Make mkstemp disposable
